before.title: 5th/6th Auxiliary Intake Port Sleeve and Actuator Seizure (NA 6-Port Induction)
before.description: All naturally aspirated FC RX-7s use Mazda's 6-port induction (6PI): two auxiliary intake ports per rotor stay closed below roughly 3,800 RPM, then rotating sleeves open them for top-end power. The vacuum/pressure-driven sleeve actuators and the sleeves themselves carbonize and seize if the car spends its life below 4,000 RPM, and the small actuator diaphragms and lines also fail with age. With the ports stuck closed the engine permanently loses roughly 25 hp above 4,000 RPM; stuck-open sleeves hurt low-end torque and idle instead.
before.solution: Free the sleeves by removing the actuators (passenger side, above the exhaust manifold), working the valve shafts loose with penetrating oil, then cleaning off all residue so they do not re-stick; badly seized sleeves require intake removal. Worn actuators can be replaced with OEM or aftermarket kits, and the accepted prevention is regularly revving the engine through the 6PI engagement range.
symptoms: Engine feels flat or breathless above 4,000 RPM
Roughly 25 hp missing at the top end
No intake note change around 3,800-4,000 RPM where 6PI should engage
Actuator rods seized — cannot be moved by hand or low air pressure
Car drives normally below 3,800 RPM

before.title: Apex seal failure and loss of compression (13B-REW rotary)
before.description: The 13B-REW twin-turbo rotary's apex seals are the single most common engine-killer on the FD. Chronic engine-bay heat, a clogged catalytic converter raising exhaust gas temps, lean running, detonation, or simple oil starvation cause the apex seals to chip, warp, or lose their airtight contact with the rotor housing. Compression drops on one or both rotors and the engine will no longer start reliably or make power. Because the rotary depends on constant seal lubrication and is intolerant of overheating and detonation, a poorly maintained 13B-REW can need a rebuild well before 60k miles, while a well-cared-for one lives past 100k. This is an age/wear and abuse-driven failure, universal to 1993-1995 FDs.
before.solution: Diagnose with a rotary compression test (a rotary-specific tester reading all three faces per rotor; healthy is roughly 100+ psi per face with even faces). Confirmed low/uneven compression means a full engine rebuild with new apex seals, corner/side seals, and housings inspected/replaced. Preventive care: keep the cooling system healthy, address the OMP/oiling, avoid lean tunes and detonation, and warm the engine before boost.
symptoms: Hard or no start when cold
Erratic or lumpy idle
Thick bluish exhaust smoke
Loss of power / low boost
Low and uneven compression readings across rotor faces

before.title: Clogged catalytic converter raising exhaust gas temps and killing the engine
before.description: Rotaries pass a lot of unburned fuel into the exhaust, so the FD's main catalytic converter is prone to clogging/breaking down with age and any oil or fuel issue upstream. A restricted cat drives exhaust gas temperatures (EGTs) sharply upward; that heat soaks back into the engine, raising internal temps and cooking the apex seals, and can lead to total engine failure. The clogging can also cause a loss of power and choke boost. This is a recognized failure chain on high-mileage 1993-1995 FDs and a reason many delete or replace the aging main cat with a high-flow unit.
before.solution: Inspect the main cat for restriction/backpressure and elevated EGTs. Replace a clogged cat with a fresh high-flow catalytic converter (or a test/replacement pipe where legal) and correct any upstream oil or fuel cause so the new unit isn't destroyed. Addressing this protects the far more expensive rotor seals.
symptoms: Noticeable loss of power / restricted feel
Elevated exhaust gas temperatures
Excess engine-bay heat
Rotten-egg smell or rattling cat internals
Secondary engine/apex seal damage if ignored

before.title: Degraded Chassis and Engine Grounds — the 3,800 RPM Hesitation
before.description: The FC's factory ground points — especially the battery ground on the driver's shock tower, which sits exposed to wheel-well water and salt, and the ECU/engine grounds — corrode with age and starve the ECU and sensors of a clean reference. The classic result is the infamous '3,800 RPM hesitation': anything from a slight hiccup to violent bucking right where the ECU brings the secondary fuel injectors online, plus hard hot starts, dim lights, and erratic gauges. Mazda acknowledged the problem in period with a service fix adding an extra ground wire to the boost/pressure sensor on early-production 1986 cars (factory-incorporated after November 1986 production).
before.solution: Clean and refresh every factory ground point (shock tower, starter/bell-housing, ECU grounds), protect them with dielectric grease, and add supplemental 8-10 gauge ground straps from the engine and chassis to the battery negative — forum consensus is this cures the hesitation about 90% of the time. If hesitation persists, clean the secondary fuel injectors and verify the 5th/6th ports (NA cars).
symptoms: Bucking or hesitation right around 3,800-4,000 RPM under acceleration
Hard or slow hot starts, lazy cranking
Dim or flickering lights and erratic gauges
Intermittent check engine light
Symptoms improve temporarily after cleaning battery terminals

before.title: DTSS Rear Toe-Control Bushing Wear — Vague, Self-Steering Rear End
before.description: The FC's Dynamic Tracking Suspension System (DTSS) uses deliberately compliant rubber bushings in the rear hub carriers so cornering loads passively steer the rear wheels (up to about one degree of toe change). After 30+ years these bushings deteriorate, and the calibrated compliance turns into uncontrolled rear toe movement: the back of the car feels vague, sloppy, or twitchy in hard corners and quick transitions, and rear alignment will not stay consistent. On a worn car the rear can feel like it steers itself mid-corner, which undermines driver confidence at speed.
before.solution: Replace the worn DTSS bushings — the near-universal fix is a Delrin/steel 'rear steer eliminator' or 'toe eliminator' bushing set (Mazdatrix, Racing Beat, etc.) pressed into the rear uprights, which removes the passive rear steer entirely and restores predictable handling. Follow with a four-wheel alignment.
symptoms: Rear end feels vague or twitchy in quick transitions and hard corners
Car seems to steer itself or wander mid-corner
Sloppy, unpredictable response during highway lane changes
Rear alignment won't hold spec / uneven rear tire wear

before.title: Fuel Pulsation Damper (FPD) failure - fuel leak and fire/lean risk
before.description: The 3rd-gen RX-7's Fuel Pulsation Damper, mounted on the fuel rail under the upper intake manifold, is a widely documented failure point that commonly lets go around 60k miles (sometimes sooner). When the FPD diaphragm fails, high-pressure fuel leaks from the fuel rails in a hidden location under the intake, which has caused numerous engine-bay fires. Even short of a fire, the resulting drop in fuel pressure leans out the front rotor and can lead to detonation and apex seal/engine damage. Affects 1993-1995 FDs.
before.solution: Inspect the FPD for fuel weeping under the upper intake. The accepted fix is to replace the FPD or install an FPD-elimination kit (block-off in place of the damper), refreshing the associated fuel rail o-rings/lines while access is open. Given the fire and lean-out risk, this is treated as a proactive replacement item on any FD of unknown history.
symptoms: Raw fuel smell in engine bay
Fuel weeping/leak under the upper intake manifold
Low or dropping fuel pressure
Lean running / front-rotor detonation
Engine-bay fire in severe cases

before.title: Hot-Start Flooding from Leaking Fuel Injectors
before.description: A widespread FD complaint is that the car becomes very hard to start after a hot soak (10–30 minutes after shutdown). Aged primary or secondary fuel injectors lose their ability to hold residual fuel pressure and drip into the rotor housings, soaking the spark plugs and flooding the engine. Because rotaries do not self-purge fuel the way a piston engine does (no intake/exhaust valves), a flooded rotary often will not start at all without a deflood procedure. Repeated flooding washes oil off the rotor seals and accelerates apex seal wear.
before.solution: Short-term deflood procedure: pull the EGI (fuel injection) fuse — typically the green 15A in the underhood fuse box — and crank for 5–10 seconds to clear fuel, then reinstall the fuse and start. Habit fix: rev to ~3,000 RPM for 10 seconds before shutdown to clear residual fuel. Permanent fix: replace the injectors (stock 550 cc primaries / 850 cc secondaries, or upgrade to RX-8 yellow secondaries or aftermarket high-impedance units). Have injectors flow-tested and cleaned if budget is tight, but old injector tips typically need replacement on a 20+ year old FD.
symptoms: Extended cranking required for hot restart
Strong fuel smell from exhaust on cranking
Engine fires briefly then dies on hot restart
Black/wet spark plugs after a failed start attempt
Battery drained from repeated cranking attempts
Easier cold-start than warm-restart

before.title: Ignition Coil and Coil Harness Failure (Leading/Trailing Misfire)
before.description: The FD3S uses four ignition coils (two leading, two trailing) wired through a long harness that runs across the hot rear of the engine bay. The coils themselves fail from heat soak, and the harness insulation cracks and shorts to ground, causing intermittent or sequential coil failures. Symptoms differ depending on which coil set fails: a failed trailing coil causes rough idle but acceptable top-end power, while a failed leading coil causes severe drivability problems but a relatively normal idle. Coil and harness failure is one of the most common drivability complaints on FDs.
before.solution: Test each coil and igniter with a multimeter against Mazda factory resistance specs. Replace failed coils with quality units (Mazdatrix re-manufactured OEM, MSD Blaster, or D585 LS truck coils with an adapter harness — popular upgrade). Critically, inspect the coil sub-harness; if insulation is cracked or wires are brittle, replace the harness or convert to a relocated dwell-controlled coil setup. Spark plugs (BUR7EQ leading / BUR9EQP trailing on stock) should be replaced at the same time and every 15,000–20,000 miles thereafter.
symptoms: Rough idle (trailing coil failure)
Misfire / loss of power under load (leading coil failure)
Engine cuts out at high RPM
Visible cracks or burn marks on coil pack body
Coil harness insulation crumbling or cracked
Replacement coils fail again within weeks (root cause is harness)

before.title: Oil Metering Pump Neglect and Brittle Injection Lines — Apex Seal Starvation
before.description: The 13B's oil metering pump (OMP) injects small amounts of engine oil to lubricate the apex and side seals; on the FC it feeds the engine through thin plastic injection lines that become rock-hard and brittle with decades of heat, cracking or snapping when disturbed. A seized pump linkage (S4 cable-actuated units), a failed electronically controlled S5 pump, or broken/leaking lines silently cuts off seal lubrication, and the consequence is accelerated apex seal wear, compression loss, and eventually engine failure. Because the engine still runs normally in the short term, the failure usually goes unnoticed until the damage is done.
before.solution: Verify the OMP actually moves and delivers oil, reseal or replace a worn pump, and replace age-hardened injection lines as preventive maintenance. Many owners instead block off the system and premix 2-stroke oil into the fuel (roughly 1 oz per 4-5 gallons), which is the accepted alternative as long as it is done every single fill-up.
symptoms: Plastic oil injection lines cracked, hardened, or weeping oil
Engine oil level never drops between changes (rotaries should consume some oil)
OMP lever or cable linkage seized or sluggish (S4 cars)
Gradual compression and power loss
Harder hot starts as seals wear

before.title: Oil Metering Pump (OMP) o-ring/line failure starving apex seals
before.description: The rotary relies 100% on the Oil Metering Pump to inject crankcase oil into the intake/combustion chambers to lubricate the apex, side, and corner seals. The OMP itself is mechanically robust, but as the FD ages its o-rings dry out and leak, the drive can fail, or the clear nylon delivery lines run empty (they should be golden-brown with oil, not clear). Any interruption in metered oil starves and burns the combustion seals, quietly leading to apex seal failure and a dead engine. This is an age/wear item on 1993-1995 FDs.
before.solution: Verify the OMP is delivering oil (check that the nylon lines are oil-stained, not empty) and reseal/rebuild the pump with fresh o-rings, or replace it. Many owners additionally premix two-stroke oil into the fuel (roughly 1-2 oz per gallon) as insurance so the seals still get lubrication if the OMP under-delivers. Keeping the OMP functional or premixing is far cheaper than the rebuild it prevents.
symptoms: Clear (empty) OMP nylon oil lines instead of oil-stained
Oil weeping from the OMP body
Higher-than-normal engine oil consumption changes
Progressive apex seal wear / compression loss

before.title: Overheating and coolant seal failure (rotor housing warp risk)
before.description: The FD's rotary rejects a lot of heat and runs on the edge thermally, so the cooling system is safety-critical: it keeps the iron/aluminum rotor housings and the rubber coolant seals from warping or failing. Common age-related causes of overheating are a worn fan clutch (overheats in stop-and-go, fine on the highway), a corroded/clogged aluminum radiator, a stuck thermostat, a corroded water pump impeller, and a missing lower underbelly/air pan (loses cooling airflow). Left unchecked, sustained overheat warps housings and cooks the coolant seals, forcing an engine rebuild. Coolant seal failure pushes combustion gases into the cooling system: coolant is expelled from the overflow, hoses go rock hard, and bubbles appear at the cap.
before.solution: Restore the cooling system as a system: replace a tired fan clutch (many convert to an electric fan), re-core or replace the radiator, fit a fresh genuine thermostat, replace the water pump on schedule, refit the underbelly pan, and flush/refill with fresh coolant on a regular interval. Bubbles at the cap, coolant pushed from the overflow, and steam clouds indicate failed coolant seals, which require an engine rebuild.
symptoms: Overheats in traffic but cools on the highway (fan clutch)
Overheats at high speed (blocked radiator / missing pan)
Coolant pushed out of overflow bottle
Bubbles in coolant when cap removed
Rock-hard coolant hoses / clouds of steam

before.title: Sequential Twin-Turbo System Failure (Solenoids, Vacuum Lines, Actuators)
before.description: The FD's sequential twin-turbo system relies on 8+ vacuum-controlled solenoids, dozens of small vacuum hoses (the infamous 'rats nest'), check valves, and two actuators to transition between primary and secondary turbo operation around 4,500 RPM. Extreme under-hood heat (often 200°F+ at idle after shutdown) hardens and cracks the rubber hoses, fails the solenoids, sticks the actuator pivots with condensation, and cracks the cast-iron turbo exhaust housings around the wastegate. Result: failure to transition (no secondary turbo), boost spikes, boost creep, fluttering between turbos, or total loss of boost.
before.solution: Pressure-test the vacuum system to locate leaks. Replace the entire vacuum hose 'rats nest' with a silicone replacement kit (correct metric ID, with Viton check valves). Bench-test each solenoid for proper actuation; replace failed solenoids individually or as a set. Free up sticky actuator pivots and reseat the secondary-turbo control arm. Inspect turbo exhaust housings for cracks — minor cracks can be left, major cracks require turbo replacement. Many owners eventually convert to a single turbo to permanently eliminate the system.
symptoms: Boost cuts out above 4,500 RPM (no transition to secondary turbo)
Fluttering or surging boost
Boost spikes above 10 psi (overboost fuel cut)
Audible vacuum leak / hissing in engine bay
Cracks visible on cast-iron turbo exhaust housings
Wastegate actuator arm disconnected or seized

before.title: Sequential twin-turbo vacuum hose failure (the "rats nest")
before.description: The FD's sequential twin-turbo system is controlled by a dense web of vacuum/pressure hoses, check valves, and solenoids nicknamed the "rats' nest." On 30-year-old cars the original silicone/rubber hoses have all reached end of life simultaneously: engine-bay heat bakes them hard, they crack, chafe through against nearby components, and pop off fittings. Any leak in this maze disrupts the changeover from the primary to the secondary turbo, so what feels like five separate boost problems is usually one aging-hose problem. Affects all 1993-1995 FDs with the stock sequential setup.
before.solution: Perform a boost/hose and check-valve diagnosis, then refresh the entire rats' nest as a set: replace all vacuum lines with fresh silicone hose, test/replace the turbo control solenoids and check valves, and verify the pressure and vacuum chambers hold. Many owners rebuild or simplify the whole system rather than chase individual leaks. Fixing one hose while leaving the rest usually just relocates the symptom.
symptoms: Boost spikes then drops / non-linear boost
Secondary turbo fails to engage at higher rpm
Flutter or surging under boost
Check Engine light for boost/turbo control
Audible vacuum leak or popped-off hose in engine bay

before.title: Trailing Ignition Drop-Out (Twin Trailing Coils, Igniter, and Select Signal)
before.description: Unlike later RX-7s, the FC fires its two trailing spark plugs through a dedicated pair of trailing coils and a separate igniter that selects T1 or T2 on the rising/falling edge of an ECU 'select' signal — a system distinct from the leading ignition. Age-failed trailing coils and igniters, corroded connectors, and poor chassis grounding at the coil/igniter mounting bracket silently kill trailing spark; the engine still starts and runs on leading ignition alone, so the failure often goes undiagnosed while the car runs rough at higher RPM with reduced power, worse fuel economy, and higher emissions. A worn crank angle sensor (chipped trigger teeth or incorrect positioning) produces similar high-RPM misbehavior and is part of the same diagnostic path.
before.solution: Test for spark at both trailing plugs, check trailing coil resistance and the igniter, and clean/verify the bracket ground and the CAS and igniter connectors; replace failed coils or igniter with known-good OEM units (commonly sourced used, as new parts are scarce). Confirm the crank angle sensor teeth are undamaged and the unit is correctly timed.
symptoms: Rough, fluttery running at higher RPM under load
Noticeable power loss and worse fuel economy
No spark at either trailing plug (T1/T2)
Failed emissions test with otherwise normal running
Erratic tachometer behavior accompanying the misfire

before.title: Turbo II Wastegate Flapper Undersizing — Boost Creep and Overboost
before.description: The Hitachi HT-18 turbocharger on the FC Turbo II uses an internal wastegate port of only about 16 mm — roughly half the size used by comparable turbos — and the small flapper door cannot bypass enough exhaust at high RPM. The result is boost creep (boost continuing to climb past the factory ceiling under sustained load) and overboost, which has been observed even on bone-stock cars and gets dramatically worse with any exhaust or intake upgrade. Uncontrolled boost leads to detonation and can destroy the rotary engine if the stock fuel system is exceeded. The earlier S4 (1987-1988) turbo is worst; S5 (1989-1991) units creep less but are still affected.
before.solution: The accepted community fix is to remove the turbo, port the wastegate orifice substantially larger, and weld on a larger flapper door that fully covers the enlarged port; many owners do this preventively before raising boost. Until fixed, keep the exhaust restriction stock and watch a known-accurate boost gauge.
symptoms: Boost keeps climbing past spec at high RPM instead of holding steady
Boost spikes or overboost cut after exhaust/downpipe upgrades
Pinging or detonation under full throttle
Bucking or sudden power cut at peak boost (overboost fuel cut)
Creep worsens in cold, dense air

before.title: Apex Seal Failure and Low Compression
before.description: The FD RX-7's 13B-REW twin-turbo rotary engine is inherently prone to apex seal wear and failure. Apex seals are the rotary equivalent of piston rings, and they wear from high temperatures, poor lubrication, and carbon buildup. Seal failure causes low compression, power loss, hard starting, and eventually a non-running engine. Even well-maintained engines typically need a rebuild between 80,000-120,000 miles.
before.solution: Prevent apex seal wear by premixing 2-stroke oil (Idemitsu premix at 1 oz per gallon of gas) in the fuel for additional lubrication. Always warm the engine fully before high-RPM driving. Never shut off a hot engine — idle for 2 minutes first. When seals fail, a full engine rebuild ($3,000-$6,000) with new apex seals, side seals, and corner seals is required. Atkins Rotary and BridgePort Machine are well-regarded rebuilders.
symptoms: Hard starting especially when hot
Loss of power and compression
Uneven idle or stalling
Excessive white smoke from exhaust
Flooding when starting (fuel washes past seals)
